hops.title: Crazy ants and the nail-polish test
hops.text: Red imported fire ants dominate most other ants by dabbing them with venom, which as an insecticide is two to three times as toxic as DDT by weight. Tawny crazy ants carry an antidote. After a hit, one curls its abdomen forward, collects formic acid from a gland at its tip with its mouth, and smears it over its body, neutralizing the venom. To test this, University of Texas researchers sealed that gland with nail polish. About half of the sealed ants died after fire ants dabbed them; 98 percent of dabbed ants with open glands survived. In the southeastern United States, crazy ants often displace fire ants.

sources.citation: LeBrun EG, Jones NT, Gilbert LE. Chemical warfare among invaders: a detoxification interaction facilitates an ant invasion. Science. 2014;343(6174):1014-1017.
Leahy C. Crazy Ants Dominate Fire Ants By Neutralizing Their Venom. UT News, The University of Texas at Austin (Feb 13, 2014).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A slim golden-brown tawny crazy ant bends its abdomen under its body to bring a clear droplet to its mouth while a red fire ant faces it on sandy soil.
image.caption: A tawny crazy ant smears its own formic acid over its body to neutralize fire ant venom.

hops.title: More fertilizer, fewer plant species
hops.text: It might seem that feeding a meadow would help more plant species share it. Since 1856, an English field has been showing otherwise. Rothamsted's Park Grass Experiment began on a pasture with about 50 plant species, and some plots get fertilizer every year. Unfertilized plots still hold 35 to 45 species. Some fertilized plots, especially those given nitrogen and phosphorus together, are down to two or three. A 2016 study of 45 grasslands on several continents found that adding more kinds of limiting nutrients left fewer species. The authors suggest that extra nutrients leave plants fewer ways to specialize on different soil resources, so fewer species can share a place.

sources.citation: Rothamsted Research. Park Grass Experiment. Electronic Rothamsted Archive (ERA).
Crawley MJ, Johnston AE, Silvertown J, et al. Determinants of species richness in the Park Grass Experiment. The American Naturalist. 2005;165(2):179-192.
Harpole WS, Sullivan LL, Lind EM, et al. Addition of multiple limiting resources reduces grassland diversity. Nature. 2016;537(7618):93-96.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A meadow split by a mowed path: a low mix of many colorful wildflowers on one side and a tall, uniform stand of grass on the other.
image.caption: At Park Grass, some fertilized plots fell from dozens of plant species to two or three.

hops.title: Stickier lizard feet in fifteen years
hops.text: In the 1990s, biologist Todd Campbell released Cuban brown anoles (Anolis sagrei) onto a few small islands in Florida's Intracoastal Waterway and kept others free of them for comparison. Within months, native green anoles (Anolis carolinensis) on the invaded islands began perching higher, above the low-perching newcomers, which also eat green anole hatchlings. About 15 years later, researchers compared islands with and without brown anoles. Green anoles living alongside them had evolved larger toepads with more sticky scales, good for gripping thinner high branches, within about 20 generations. Lead author Yoel Stuart compared the pace to average American men going from 5 foot 9 to 6 foot 4.

sources.citation: Stuart YE, Campbell TS, Hohenlohe PA, Reynolds RG, Revell LJ, Losos JB. Rapid evolution of a native species following invasion by a congener. Science. 2014;346(6208):463-466.
Reuell P. Rapid-fire evolution. The Harvard Gazette (Nov 4, 2014).
Leahy C. Florida Lizards Evolve Rapidly, Within 15 Years and 20 Generations. UT News, The University of Texas at Austin (Oct 23, 2014).

image.caption: Pushed higher by brown anoles, Florida green anoles evolved larger, stickier toepads in about 20 generations.

audio.title: Antidotes, sour nectar and sticky feet
audio.transcript:
Competition in this lesson lives in a few tidy equations. Out in the world, competitors get a lot more inventive. Here are three real cases.

First, a chemical fight between two invading ants. Across the southern United States, red imported fire ants dominate most other ants, and they do it directly. A fire ant dabs a rival with venom that, as an insecticide, is two to three times as toxic as D D T by weight. Most ants back off. Tawny crazy ants do not. When a crazy ant gets dabbed, it curls its abdomen forward, picks up a drop of its own formic acid with its mouth, and smears it across its body. The acid neutralizes the venom. Researchers at the University of Texas wanted to know what happens when a crazy ant cannot treat itself, so they sealed the acid gland with nail polish. Yes, nail polish. After a dab of fire ant venom, about half of the sealed ants died. Among dabbed ants whose glands were left open, ninety-eight percent survived. In the southeastern United States, crazy ants now often push fire ants out. That is interference competition: one competitor acting straight on another.

Second, a case where arriving first gives either competitor the edge. It echoes the lesson's model, where the starting numbers can decide the winner. It happens inside a single flower. Along the California coast, fresh nectar of the sticky monkeyflower averages around p H seven point five, close to neutral. Hummingbirds carry microbes from flower to flower. If a bacterium called Acinetobacter nectaris gets there first, it drives the nectar down to around p H three, sour enough to strongly hold back the common nectar yeast, Metschnikowia reukaufii. If the yeast arrives first, it may use up amino acids the bacteria need, and the bacteria struggle instead. When Stanford-led researchers sampled one thousand one hundred and fifty-two wild flowers, they often found a flower dominated by bacteria or by yeast, but rarely by both. In one field test, they tucked P C R tubes of artificial nectar into artificial flowers on garden stakes. Visitors, mostly hummingbirds, drank less of the most acidic nectar. Whichever microbe arrives first tends to own the flower.

Third, competitors that moved apart while scientists watched. In the nineteen nineties, biologist Todd Campbell released Cuban brown anoles onto a few small islands in Florida's Intracoastal Waterway, and kept other islands free of them for comparison. Within months, the native green anoles on invaded islands started perching higher in the trees, above the brown anoles. Adults of both species also eat the other's hatchlings, so predation is another possible reason for the shift, alongside competition for food and space. About fifteen years later, researchers compared islands with and without brown anoles. Green anoles living alongside them had evolved larger toepads with more sticky scales, good for gripping thinner branches up high, within about twenty generations. The lead author, Yoel Stuart, put the pace in human terms: it is like average American men going from about five foot nine to about six foot four in twenty generations.

An ant with an antidote, a microbe that sours a flower, a lizard that grew stickier feet. Each time, the question is the one this lesson keeps asking: who can hold a place when a rival is already there?
